label: Keeping a Confidence
framing: When someone tells you a hard thing, they hand you a piece of themselves to hold. Scripture is plain that a faithful person covers it, while the gossip spreads it for the small thrill of being the one who knows. The tongue that cannot keep a secret is not merely indiscreet. It has broken trust, and the wreckage often cannot be rebuilt.
cultural: In the close world of the village and the early church, where everyone knew everyone, a loose tongue could ruin a name beyond recovery, which is why the wisdom writers return to it again and again. Our age has built the gossip machine to a scale they could not have imagined, the screenshot, the group chat, the post, where a confidence betrayed travels farther in an hour than a village rumor did in a year, and we still call it harmless.
historical: The book of Proverbs, gathered under Solomon around 950 BC and after, warns repeatedly against the whisperer who separates close friends. The monastic rule of Benedict in the sixth century placed heavy weight on guarding the tongue as a discipline of the whole life. The seal of confession, by which a priest may never reveal what is told him, grew from the conviction that some words are held in absolute trust, even unto death.
application: When someone shares something in confidence, treat it as theirs and not yours, and do not pass it along under the cover of a prayer request. If you are uncertain whether you may repeat a thing, ask, or assume you may not. Refuse to be the audience for gossip, since the one who carries tales to you will carry yours away. And guard the words shared with you as you would want your own guarded.

verses.text: A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence.
verses.where: A gossip reveals a secret, but a trustworthy person keeps a confidence. The proverb sets the two side by side as two kinds of people, and the site's note places it in a chapter about honest dealing, from the marketplace to the city. What is told in trust is treated like something weighed on honest scales.

verses.text: But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.
verses.where: After the shepherds tell everyone what the angels said, Mary treasures up all these things and ponders them in her heart. The site's note says Luke sets her lasting reflection against the crowd's passing amazement, and the plain note says the shepherds' telling and Mary's quiet pondering are both ways of receiving good news. Not everything a person knows needs saying aloud.

verses.text: Argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another’s confidence, lest the one who hears may disgrace you, and your infamy never go away.
verses.where: Argue your case with your neighbor without betraying another's confidence, the proverb says, or the one who hears may disgrace you and the shame will not go away. The site's note sets it among the Hezekiah collection's sayings on words well spoken and restraint. Even in a real quarrel, what someone else told you in trust is not yours to use.

verses.text: A perverse man spreads dissension, and a gossip divides close friends.
verses.where: A perverse man spreads dissension, and a gossip divides close friends. The site's note places it in a chapter of famous sayings, including pleasant words and pride before a fall. A broken confidence rarely harms only one person; it splits the friendships around it.

verses.text: Without wood, a fire goes out; without gossip, a conflict ceases.
verses.where: Without wood a fire goes out, and without gossip a conflict ceases. The site's note says the end of the chapter exposes the meddler, the gossip and the quarreler. A quarrel can be starved simply by not passing on what was said.

verses.text: Finally, after she had pressed him daily with her words and pleaded until he was sick to death, Samson told her all that was in his heart: “My hair has never been cut, because I have been a Nazirite to God from my mother’s womb. If I am shaved, my strength will leave me, and I will become as weak as any other man.” When Delilah realized that he had revealed to her all that was in his heart, she sent this message to the lords of the Philistines: “Come up once more, for he has revealed to me all that is in his heart.” Then the lords of the Philistines came to her, bringing the money in their hands.
verses.where: Pressed by Delilah day after day, Samson tells her all that is in his heart, and she sends at once for the Philistine lords, who come with the money in their hands. The site's note on the chapter says she was paid by the Philistine lords to discover his secret. The oldest betrayal of a confidence in Scripture was sold for silver.

verses.text: You must not go about spreading slander among your people. You must not endanger the life of your neighbor. I am the LORD.
verses.where: The law forbids going about spreading slander among the people or endangering a neighbor's life, and ends, I am the LORD. The site's note says the chapter grounds every command in God's own character, with love of neighbor at its center. Careless talk about a neighbor is set beside harm to his life.

verses.text: If anyone considers himself religious and yet does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless.
verses.where: James says that if anyone considers himself religious and does not bridle his tongue, he deceives his heart and his religion is worthless. The site's note on the chapter says a believer's religion shows in controlled speech and care for orphans and widows. A loose tongue is not a small fault in a religious person; James says it empties the religion.

verses.text: If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.
verses.where: Jesus says that if a brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. The site's plain note says he sends you to the person, not to everyone else about the person, and asks whether there is someone you have talked about rather than talked to. The site's note adds that this never requires a victim of abuse to confront the abuser alone.

verses.text: No longer do I call you servants, for a servant does not understand what his master is doing. But I have called you friends, because everything I have learned from My Father I have made known to you.
verses.where: Jesus tells his disciples that he no longer calls them servants but friends, because everything he learned from his Father he has made known to them. The site's note says a slave is not told his master's purposes, and Jesus has told them everything. Friendship, in his words, is being trusted with what is close to the heart.

misread.taken: Whoever conceals an offense promotes love is used to keep abuse secret, as if love meant never telling, and a person who reports harm were the one breaking the peace.
misread.says: The site's plain note on 1 Corinthians 13, where love bears all things, a word that can mean to cover, says Paul is not telling anyone to hide abuse, to keep quiet about harm, or to stay where they are in danger, and that crimes should be reported to the authorities. Its note on Matthew 18 says abuse and other crimes are reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. The proverb's other half warns against bringing up a friend's past offense to divide friends; it does not ask anyone to cover for harm.
misread.text: Whoever conceals an offense promotes love, but he who brings it up separates friends.

whole: If what someone has told you is that they or a child are being harmed, or that they intend to harm themselves or someone else, that is not a confidence to keep alone: tell someone who can help, and the site's notes say abuse and crimes belong with the proper authorities. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Most of us have been on both sides of a broken confidence. A friend tells you something hard, a debt, a diagnosis, a marriage in trouble, a sin they are ashamed of, and a week later you hear it back from someone else, sometimes as a prayer request. Or you are the one who passed it on, telling yourself it was concern, or that this one person would not repeat it. Some people have stopped telling anyone anything because of what happened the last time.

Scripture names what is underneath it. Proverbs says a gossip reveals a secret and divides close friends, and that a quarrel dies down without gossip as a fire goes out without wood. Delilah learned what was in Samson's heart and sold it to the Philistine lords. Few of us sell a secret for silver; we trade it for something smaller, the feeling of being the one who knows, a moment of attention, a way to look better beside someone else. James says that if anyone thinks himself religious and does not bridle his tongue, his religion is worthless. That is a hard word for churches where much is passed on in the language of concern, and most of us have spoken that language.

So the Bible's wisdom is simple and costly. A trustworthy person keeps a confidence. When you have a grievance, take it to the person, not to everyone else about the person, as Jesus says in Matthew 18, and argue your case with your neighbor without betraying what someone else told you. Before passing something on, ask whether the person would want it known, and whether you are helping or only telling. Mary treasured things and pondered them in her heart; not everything a person knows needs to be said. But a confidence is never a reason to hide harm. If someone is being hurt, the faithful thing is to get help, and the site's notes are plain that crimes and abuse are reported to the proper authorities.

The hope Scripture gives is a friend who can be trusted with everything. Jesus told his disciples that he called them friends, because everything he had heard from his Father he had made known to them. The site's note on Psalm 139 says God knows the worst about us and has not let go. A person who has been trusted and known like that can learn to be trustworthy, and a church where confidences are kept becomes a place where people can finally tell the truth.
deep.sit: Is there something you were told in trust that you have been tempted to pass on, and what would keeping it, or rightly getting help with it, look like this week?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note calls Psalm 141 a good evening prayer: at the end of the day, ask God to guard your mouth and your heart.
prayer.text: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips. Do not let my heart be drawn to any evil thing or take part in works of wickedness with men who do iniquity; let me not feast on their delicacies.

careLines.text: He is not telling anyone to hide abuse, to keep quiet about harm, or to stay where they are in danger.
It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
